---
title: "Conjoint Experiments as Paired Comparisons"
description: |
  A conjoint experiment asks people to choose between pairs of randomly built
  profiles: two immigrants, two candidates, two vaccines. The usual summary is
  the average effect of each attribute. Read as item response data, each choice
  is a paired comparison, which lets us ask one measurement question across
  every conjoint experiment in IRW: how much do a profile's attributes predict
  the choice of a respondent nobody has seen yet? Start by taking one of the
  experiments yourself.
date: today
bibliography: conjoint_data/references.bib
format:
  html:
    code-fold: true
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 2
execute:
  echo: true
  message: false
  warning: false
---

pretty_attr <- function(a) {
  x <- gsub("_", " ", sub("^attr_", "", a))
  paste0(toupper(substr(x, 1, 1)), substr(x, 2, nchar(x)))
}
# A lookup into one of the lists above, falling back per element.
lk <- function(lst, tb, key, default) {
  m <- lst[[tb]]
  got <- if (is.null(m)) rep(NA_character_, length(key)) else unname(m[key])
  ifelse(is.na(got), default, got)
}

## Motivation

A conjoint experiment shows a respondent two profiles side by side and asks
which one they prefer. Each profile is a bundle of attributes (an immigrant's
education, profession, country of origin and so on), and every attribute is
drawn at random, independently for each profile. The respondent sees a handful
of such pairs. Because the attributes are randomized, comparing how often
profiles with one level are chosen against profiles with another level
estimates that level's average effect on the choice, the *average marginal
component effect* or AMCE [@Hainmueller_2014]. The design is popular in
political science because it lets one experiment estimate the effects of many
attributes at once.

The easiest way to see how this works is to take part in one. The card below
deals real pairs from four IRW experiments, and the menu switches between them:
immigrants applying for admission to the United States
[@Hainmueller_2014], packages of terms for Colombia's peace agreement with the
FARC [@Tellez_2021], packs of barley flour in Scottish shops
[@https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15420092], and Democratic candidates for state office
[@Laterzo_Tingley_2024]. Each time, choose the one you would pick. After each
choice you will see what the person who actually saw that pair chose, and the
chart below the card turns your choices into AMCEs and sets them against the
estimates from everybody who took that experiment. Your choices are kept per
experiment, so you can switch and come back.

The four are readable as a card -- a handful of attributes, short labels -- and
they differ in how much their attributes turn out to explain, which is what the
rest of the page is about. Taking two of them back to back is the quickest way
to feel that difference: in the flour experiment the price alone nearly settles
the choice, while in the candidate experiment nothing printed on the card moves
it much.

```{r}
#| label: widget-data
#| echo: false

w_levels <- bind_rows(lapply(widget_tables, function(tb) {
  x <- widget_levels |> filter(table == tb)
  x |> mutate(
    attr_label = lk(attr_labels, tb, attribute, pretty_attr(attribute)),
    card       = card_fix(lk(card_labels, tb, level, level)),
    short      = card_fix(lk(level_labels, tb, level, card)))
})) |>
  arrange(table, ord_attr, ord_level) |>
  group_by(table) |>
  mutate(row = row_number()) |>
  ungroup()

w_support <- widget_support |>
  mutate(other = ifelse(is.na(other), "", other)) |>
  unnest_longer(other_levels, keep_empty = TRUE) |>
  mutate(other_levels = ifelse(is.na(other_levels), "", other_levels))

w_info <- widget_info |>
  inner_join(widget_meta, by = "table") |>
  inner_join(widget_ref |> group_by(table) |> summarise(ref_max = max(abs(ref))), by = "table") |>
  mutate(
    n_resp_txt = format(n_resp, big.mark = ","),
    x_label    = paste0("Change in the chance ",
                        ifelse(grepl("^[AEIOU]", noun), "an ", "a "),
                        tolower(noun), " is chosen"),
    # HHY's reference points are the published AMCEs (which the IRW table
    # reproduces exactly); every other experiment's are the same difference in
    # choice rates the widget computes, taken over all of its respondents.
    ref_label  = ifelse(table == example_table,
                        paste0("the published AMCEs from ", n_resp_txt, " respondents"),
                        paste0("the same estimates from all ", n_resp_txt, " respondents")),
    is_example = table == example_table) |>
  arrange(match(table, widget_tables))

ojs_define(w_tasks_r = widget_tasks, w_ref_r = widget_ref, w_levels_r = w_levels,
           w_support_r = w_support, w_info_r = w_info)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

w_tasks_all   = transpose(w_tasks_r)
w_ref_all     = transpose(w_ref_r)
w_levels_all  = transpose(w_levels_r)
w_support_all = transpose(w_support_r)
w_info_all    = transpose(w_info_r)

viewof w_table = Inputs.select(w_info_all.map(d => d.table), {
  label: "Experiment",
  value: w_info_all[0].table,
  width: 560,
  format: t => w_info_all.find(d => d.table === t).label
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

w_info   = w_info_all.find(d => d.table === w_table)
w_levels = w_levels_all.filter(d => d.table === w_table)
w_ref    = w_ref_all.filter(d => d.table === w_table)

// the selected experiment's attributes, in the order the card lists them
w_attrs = Array.from(d3.group(w_levels, d => d.attribute), ([a, v]) => ({
  attribute: a, label: v[0].attr_label, ord: v[0].ord_attr
})).sort((x, y) => x.ord - y.ord)

// one entry per task: [profile 1, profile 2], each a map from attribute to
// level, in a random order for this reader
w_pairs = {
  const rows = w_tasks_all.filter(d => d.table === w_table);
  const pairs = Array.from(d3.group(rows, d => d.task_key).values()).map(rs =>
    Array.from(d3.group(rs, d => d.profile), ([pr, v]) => ({
      profile: pr, choice: v[0].choice, vals: new Map(v.map(r => [r.attribute, r.value]))
    })).sort((a, b) => a.profile - b.profile));
  return d3.shuffle(pairs.slice());
}

// the card's text for a level, and the chart's short label
w_card  = new Map(w_levels.map(d => [d.attribute + "|" + d.level, d.card]))
w_short = new Map(w_levels.map(d => [d.attribute + "|" + d.level, d.short]))
w_base  = new Map(w_levels.filter(d => d.baseline).map(d => [d.attribute, d.level]))

// for each non-baseline level: the restricted partner attributes, and which of
// their values the level is compared over (a level with no restriction has none)
w_rules = {
  const m = new Map();
  for (const s of w_support_all.filter(d => d.table === w_table && d.other !== "")) {
    const k = s.attribute + "|" + s.level;
    if (!m.has(k)) m.set(k, new Map());
    const byOther = m.get(k);
    if (!byOther.has(s.other)) byOther.set(s.other, new Set());
    if (s.other_levels !== "") byOther.get(s.other).add(s.other_levels);
  }
  return m;
}

// Answers are kept per experiment, so switching away and back does not lose
// them. This cell does not depend on the menu, so the store survives a switch.
cj_store = new Map()
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

viewof w_answers = {
  const tab = w_table, attrs = w_attrs, pairs = w_pairs, question = w_info.question;
  const el = html`<div class="cj-widget"></div>`;
  if (!cj_store.has(tab)) cj_store.set(tab, []);
  el.value = cj_store.get(tab);
  let i = el.value.length, last = null;
  const cell = (txt) => html`<td style="padding:4px 10px;border-top:1px solid #ddd;">${txt}</td>`;
  function render() {
    const pair = pairs[i % pairs.length];
    const pick = (p) => {
      last = {mine: p, theirs: pair[0].choice === 1 ? 1 : 2};
      el.value = [...el.value, {pair, chosen: p}];
      cj_store.set(tab, el.value);
      i += 1;
      el.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
      render();
    };
    const btn = (p) => {
      const b = html`<button class="btn btn-outline-primary btn-sm">Choose ${w_info.noun.toLowerCase()} ${p}</button>`;
      b.onclick = () => pick(p);
      return b;
    };
    const fb = last === null ? "" :
      `On the last pair you chose ${w_info.noun.toLowerCase()} ${last.mine}; the respondent who saw it chose ${last.theirs === last.mine ? "the same one." : `${w_info.noun.toLowerCase()} ${last.theirs}.`}`;
    const agree = el.value.filter(a => (a.pair[0].choice === 1 ? 1 : 2) === a.chosen).length;
    el.replaceChildren(html`<div>
      <p style="margin-bottom:6px;"><strong>Pair ${i + 1}.</strong> ${question}</p>
      <table style="border-collapse:collapse;max-width:760px;width:100%;font-size:0.92em;">
        <thead><tr><th></th><th style="padding:4px 10px;">${w_info.noun} 1</th><th style="padding:4px 10px;">${w_info.noun} 2</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody>${attrs.map(a => html`<tr>${cell(html`<strong>${a.label}</strong>`)}${
          pair.map(pf => cell(w_card.get(a.attribute + "|" + pf.vals.get(a.attribute))))}</tr>`)}</tbody>
        <tfoot><tr><td></td><td style="padding:8px 10px;">${btn(1)}</td><td style="padding:8px 10px;">${btn(2)}</td></tr></tfoot>
      </table>
      <p style="margin-top:6px;color:#555;font-size:0.9em;">${fb}${el.value.length ? ` You have made ${el.value.length} choice${el.value.length > 1 ? "s" : ""} in this experiment and agreed with the original respondent on ${agree}.` : ""}</p>
    </div>`);
  }
  render();
  return el;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

// The reader's estimates: for each level, the share of profiles with that level
// the reader chose, minus the share for the baseline level. Where the design
// restricted which profiles could appear, the comparison is made only among
// profiles where both levels were possible, which is what makes the simple
// difference an AMCE.
w_mine = {
  const profs = w_answers.flatMap(a => a.pair.map(p => ({vals: p.vals, chosen: p.profile === a.chosen ? 1 : 0})));
  const ref = new Map(w_ref.map(d => [d.attribute + "|" + d.level, d]));
  return w_levels.filter(d => !d.baseline).map(d => {
    const key = d.attribute + "|" + d.level;
    const rule = w_rules.get(key);
    const ok = p => !rule || Array.from(rule).every(([z, allowed]) => allowed.has(p.vals.get(z)));
    const g1 = profs.filter(p => ok(p) && p.vals.get(d.attribute) === d.level);
    const g0 = profs.filter(p => ok(p) && p.vals.get(d.attribute) === w_base.get(d.attribute));
    const r = ref.get(key);
    const out = {...d, ref: r ? r.ref : null, ref_se: r ? r.ref_se : null};
    if (!g1.length || !g0.length) return {...out, mine: null};
    const sh = g => (d3.sum(g, p => p.chosen) + 0.5) / (g.length + 1);
    const est = d3.mean(g1, p => p.chosen) - d3.mean(g0, p => p.chosen);
    const se = Math.sqrt(sh(g1) * (1 - sh(g1)) / g1.length + sh(g0) * (1 - sh(g0)) / g0.length);
    return {...out, mine: est, lo: est - 2 * se, hi: est + 2 * se};
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

{
  const n = w_answers.length;
  const lab = d => d.attr_label + ": " + d.short;
  const rows = w_levels.map(lab);
  const pub = w_mine.filter(d => d.ref !== null);
  const base = w_levels.filter(d => d.baseline);
  const mine = w_mine.filter(d => d.mine !== null);
  const xs = mine.map(d => d.mine), ys = mine.map(d => d.ref);
  const mx = d3.mean(xs), my = d3.mean(ys);
  const cor = xs.length > 5 ? d3.sum(xs.map((x, i) => (x - mx) * (ys[i] - my))) /
    Math.sqrt(d3.sum(xs.map(x => (x - mx) ** 2)) * d3.sum(ys.map(y => (y - my) ** 2))) : null;
  const note = n < 5
    ? `Make at least five choices to see your estimates (${n} so far).`
    : `Your estimates from ${n} choices (red, ±2 SE) against ${w_info.ref_label} (blue, ±2 SE)` +
      (cor !== null && isFinite(cor) ? `. Across the ${mine.length} levels you have estimates for, the two correlate at r = ${cor.toFixed(2)}.` : ".");
  const m = Math.min(1, Math.max(0.5, 1.1 * w_info.ref_max));
  // room for the longest row label, which varies a lot between experiments
  const marginLeft = Math.min(340, Math.max(180, 6.4 * d3.max(rows, r => r.length)));
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width: Math.max(760, marginLeft + 440),
    height: 22 * rows.length + 40,
    marginLeft,
    x: {label: w_info.x_label, domain: [-m, m], grid: true},
    clip: true,
    y: {domain: rows, label: null},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "#999"}),
      Plot.dot(base, {x: 0, y: lab, symbol: "diamond", fill: "white", stroke: "#333", strokeWidth: 1.5, r: 5, title: () => "Baseline level"}),
      n >= 5 ? Plot.ruleY(mine, {y: lab, x1: "lo", x2: "hi", stroke: "#d73027", strokeOpacity: 0.5}) : null,
      n >= 5 ? Plot.dot(mine, {x: "mine", y: lab, fill: "#d73027", r: 3.5,
        title: d => `You: ${d.mine.toFixed(2)}\nAll respondents: ${d.ref.toFixed(2)}`}) : null,
      Plot.ruleY(pub, {y: lab, x1: d => d.ref - 2 * d.ref_se, x2: d => d.ref + 2 * d.ref_se,
        stroke: "#2166ac", strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.dot(pub, {x: "ref", y: lab, fill: "#2166ac", r: 3.5,
        title: d => `All respondents: ${d.ref.toFixed(3)}`})
    ]
  });
  return html`<div><p style="font-size:0.92em;color:#333;">${note}</p>${plot}</div>`;
}
```

Diamonds mark each attribute's baseline level, against which the others are
measured. Two things stand out after ten or twenty choices. Your own estimates
are noisy: the original respondents each made about five choices, which is very
little information about one person, while the reference estimates pool hundreds
or thousands of people. And in three of the four experiments the pooled effects
are modest next to that noise. In the immigration experiment none of them moves
the chance of admission by more than
`r round(max(abs(hhy_amce$published_amce)), 2)`, and in the candidate experiment
no attribute moves the chance of a vote by more than
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(widget_ref$ref[widget_ref$table == "laterzotingley_2024_crime_national"])))`;
the flour is the exception, where moving from the cheapest to the dearest pack
costs it
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(widget_ref$ref[widget_ref$table == "chen_2025_bere_barley_scot"])))`
of its chance of being bought.

```{r}
#| label: hhy-check
#| echo: false

hhy_diff <- max(abs(hhy_amce$irw_amce - hhy_amce$published_amce), na.rm = TRUE)
hhy_se_diff <- max(abs(hhy_amce$irw_se - hhy_amce$published_se), na.rm = TRUE)
hhy_dim_diff <- max(abs(hhy_amce$dim - hhy_amce$irw_amce), na.rm = TRUE)
```

The published estimates plotted here are not borrowed: all
`r sum(!hhy_amce$baseline)` of them, and their standard errors, come back out of
the IRW table `hainmueller_2014_immigrant` to
`r if (max(hhy_diff, hhy_se_diff) < 1e-10) "at least ten decimal places" else signif(max(hhy_diff, hhy_se_diff), 1)`,
that is, exactly. The [conjoint standard](../conjoint_standard.qmd) shows how to
read a conjoint table and fit the model that gives them. The simple difference
in choice rates the widget uses, applied to all 1,396 respondents, is within
`r round(hhy_dim_diff, 3)` of every AMCE.

The rest of this page steps back from the average effects and asks a
predictive question instead. Read as item response data, each task is a paired
comparison: two objects, one chosen. That is the same shape as the
[comparisons](intransitivity.qmd) elsewhere in IRW, except that the objects are
built at random rather than fixed. So we can ask: **how much do the attributes
explain?** How much better than a coin flip does a model of the attributes
predict the choices of a respondent it was not fitted to? We score that with
the InterModel Vigorish [IMV, @domingue2025imv; @domingue2024imvlens], which the
[IMV vignette](imv.qmd) introduces, and we ask it of every eligible conjoint
experiment in IRW and of the item side of the warehouse for comparison.

## Data and methods

### Dataset selection

The IRW conjoint source holds `r r_n_conj` tables across its two shards. We use
those with a forced choice between exactly two profiles and at least 500
usable tasks. A task is one choice screen: a respondent sees a pair of
profiles and picks one, so a study with 1,000 respondents who each saw five
pairs has 5,000 tasks. A usable task is one in which exactly one of the two
profiles was chosen, which drops opt-outs and unanswered screens. The 500 is a
total over all respondents, not a count per respondent:

```{r}
#| label: filter-datasets
#| eval: false

meta <- read.csv(paste0("https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.irw_meta:v44_0.",
                        "conj_metadata/rows?format=csv"))
candidates <- subset(meta, grepl("(^|;)choice(;|$)", outcomes) & n_profiles == 2 &
                           n_respondents * n_tasks >= 500)$table
```

`r r_all_candidates` tables met this screen as of
`r format(date_run, "%B %Y")`, `r if (r_n_tables_run == r_all_candidates) "all of them with" else paste(r_n_tables_run, "with")`
at least 500 usable tasks. Tables with more than 5,000 respondents were subsampled to 5,000 at
random.

### Per-table computation

For each table, the two profiles in a task are coded as attribute dummies and
the model works with their difference, so a task becomes one binary outcome:
was the first profile chosen? Attributes that were not shown on a profile get
a level of their own.

The choice is then regressed on the difference in attribute dummies by
L2-penalised logistic regression (penalty 1, intercept unpenalised), fitted on
four fifths of the respondents and used to predict the other fifth, rotating
over five folds. The baseline is a coin weighted to the training share of
first-profile choices, and the IMV compares the two. Whole respondents are held
out, so the number says how well a design's attributes predict the choices of
someone the model has never seen.

### The item side, for comparison

An IMV of some size is hard to read on its own, so we compute the same quantity
on ordinary item response data, where the counterpart of an attribute is an
item. We sampled `r r_irt_sampled` tables at random from the `r r_irt_pool`
dichotomous core IRW tables that are cross-sectional, at least 90% complete,
and have 300 to 20,000 respondents and 5 to 100 items. The design is the one
above with items in place of attributes: whole persons are held out, a fifth at
a time; the model is each item's difficulty, the logit of its mean among the
training persons; and the baseline is a coin weighted to the training share of
correct or endorsed responses. `r nrow(irt_df)` of the `r r_irt_sampled` gave
results (a table whose responses turn out not to be dichotomous is dropped).

The two sides are not two estimates of one quantity. Each says, for one kind of
design, how much the features of the thing being judged predict a stranger's
response to it.

::: {.callout-note}
To reproduce with current IRW holdings, re-run `conjoint_compute.R`
and commit the updated `conjoint_data/conjoint_results.rds`. Every table is read
without a login.
:::

## Results

### One experiment, worked through

Start with one experiment, the immigration study the card opens on (the
arithmetic below is for that one whichever you took). Fitting the model above to
`hainmueller_2014_immigrant` -- on four fifths of the 1,396 respondents at a
time, predicting the fifth left out -- gives a held-out probability for each of
its `r format(nrow(example_pred), big.mark = ",")` tasks: the chance that this
respondent, whose choices the model never saw, picked the first of the two
applicants. The model is often fairly sure. Its predictions run from
`r round(100 * quantile(example_pred$p_attr, 0.05))`% to
`r round(100 * quantile(example_pred$p_attr, 0.95))`% at the fifth and
ninety-fifth percentiles, and across that range they are about right.

```{r}
#| label: fig-example-cal
#| fig-cap: "Held-out predictions for `hainmueller_2014_immigrant`, grouped into ten equal bins: the model's average predicted probability that the first applicant was admitted against the share of those tasks in which the respondent did admit them. Points on the diagonal are predictions that come true at the rate claimed. Point size is the number of tasks in the bin."

cal <- example_pred |>
  mutate(bin = ntile(p_attr, 10)) |>
  group_by(bin) |>
  summarise(pred = mean(p_attr), obs = mean(y), n = n())

ggplot(cal, aes(pred, obs)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = irw_grey) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = irw_blue, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 5, guide = "none") +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Predicted chance the first applicant is admitted",
       y = "Share actually admitted")
```

To turn that into one number we compare two predictions of the same held-out
choices: the attribute model, and a coin weighted to the share of
first-applicant choices in the training respondents. The IMV converts each
model's average log-likelihood into the accuracy of a weighted coin that would
earn it, and reports the relative gain.

```{r}
#| label: example-imv
#| echo: true

mean_ll <- function(y, p) mean(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p))

# The accuracy w of a coin whose log-likelihood matches this model's.
w_of <- function(ll) {
  if (ll <= log(0.5)) return(0.5)
  uniroot(function(w) w * log(w) + (1 - w) * log(1 - w) - ll, c(0.5, 1 - 1e-12))$root
}

ll_base <- mean_ll(example_pred$y, example_pred$p_base)   # weighted coin
ll_attr <- mean_ll(example_pred$y, example_pred$p_attr)   # attribute model
w_base  <- w_of(ll_base)
w_attr  <- w_of(ll_attr)
imv     <- (w_attr - w_base) / w_base
c(ll_base = ll_base, ll_attr = ll_attr, w_base = w_base, w_attr = w_attr, imv = imv)
```

```{r}
#| label: example-numbers
#| echo: false

ex_pct <- mean(summary_df$imv_attr < summary_df$imv_attr[summary_df$table == example_table])
```

The applicants' attributes are randomized, so the coin is right
`r round(100 * w_base)`% of the time -- which is what makes a conjoint a clean
test. The attribute model predicts these choices like a coin that comes up
right `r round(100 * w_attr, 1)`% of the time, and the IMV is the gain over the
baseline on that scale: `r sprintf("%.2f", imv)`. Nine attributes, none of which
moves the average chance of admission by more than
`r round(max(abs(hhy_amce$published_amce)), 2)`, together carry half again as
much predictive accuracy as knowing nothing at all.

That is a lot, and this experiment is not typical:
`r round(100 * ex_pct)`% of the conjoint experiments in IRW come out below it.


```{r}
#| label: q1-numbers
#| echo: false

q1 <- summary_df |> filter(!is.na(imv_attr))
q1_med <- median(q1$imv_attr)
q1_qu  <- quantile(q1$imv_attr, c(0.1, 0.9))
q1_w   <- median(q1$w_attr)
q1_wb  <- median(q1$w_base)
q1_rho <- cor(q1$imv_attr, q1$n_attr, method = "spearman")
q1_hi  <- q1 |> slice_max(imv_attr, n = 1)
```

### How much do the attributes explain?

Across `r nrow(q1)` experiments the median IMV of the attribute model over a
coin flip is `r sprintf("%.2f", q1_med)`. In accuracy terms, the median attribute model
predicts a held-out choice like a coin that comes up right
`r round(100 * q1_w)`% of the time, against `r round(100 * q1_wb)`% for the
baseline. That is a substantial amount for a randomly assembled bundle of five
or ten features: knowing nothing about a respondent, and only what the two
profiles look like, gets you most of the way from a coin flip to two choices in
three.

The spread is wide. Eight in ten experiments fall between
`r round(q1_qu[1], 2)` and `r round(q1_qu[2], 2)`, and designs with more
attributes are not more predictable (Spearman $\rho$ = `r round(q1_rho, 2)`
between the IMV and the number of attributes). More attributes give the model
more to work with but also more ways for a respondent to trade one against
another, and the two appear to cancel.

```{r}
#| label: fig-q1
#| fig-cap: "Held-out IMV of the attribute model over a coin flip, one point per experiment, by the number of attributes in the design. The dashed line marks the median. The red points are the four experiments the card above offers, which were picked to span this range. Hover for the table."

# The four experiments a reader can take, labelled in the words the menu uses.
q1_widget <- q1 |>
  filter(table %in% widget_tables) |>
  left_join(tibble(table = c("hainmueller_2014_immigrant", "tellez_2021_peace_packages",
                             "chen_2025_bere_barley_scot", "laterzotingley_2024_crime_national"),
                   tag = c("immigrants", "peace agreements", "barley flour", "candidates")),
            by = "table")
p1 <- ggplot(q1, aes(n_attr, imv_attr,
                     text = paste0(table, "<br>IMV = ", round(imv_attr, 3),
                                   "<br>attributes: ", n_attr, "<br>usable tasks: ", n_tasks_used))) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, colour = irw_blue, alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = q1_med, linetype = "dashed", colour = irw_grey) +
  geom_point(data = q1_widget, colour = irw_red, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = "Number of attributes", y = "IMV, attributes over a coin flip")

# ggplotly centres geom_text, so the four tags are plotly annotations instead,
# anchored to the right of their point.
ggplotly(p1, tooltip = "text") |>
  layout(annotations = lapply(seq_len(nrow(q1_widget)), function(i) list(
    x = q1_widget$n_attr[i], y = q1_widget$imv_attr[i], text = q1_widget$tag[i],
    xref = "x", yref = "y", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "middle", xshift = 8,
    showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = irw_red, size = 11),
    bgcolor = "rgba(255,255,255,0.78)", borderpad = 1)))
```

### Against the item side of the warehouse

```{r}
#| label: cmp-numbers
#| echo: false

irt_med  <- median(irt_df$imv_item)
irt_wb   <- median(irt_df$w_base)
irt_w    <- median(irt_df$w_item)
both <- bind_rows(
  q1 |> transmute(table, imv = imv_attr, family = "Conjoint: profile attributes",
                  detail = paste0("attributes: ", n_attr, "; usable tasks: ", n_tasks_used)),
  irt_df |> transmute(table, imv = imv_item, family = "Item response: item difficulties",
                      detail = paste0("items: ", items, "; persons: ", persons)))
```

An IMV of `r sprintf("%.2f", q1_med)` is easier to read next to the same quantity
computed the same way on ordinary item response data. There, across
`r nrow(irt_df)` dichotomous tables, knowing which item a person is answering
raises held-out prediction by a median IMV of `r round(irt_med, 3)`, roughly a
quarter of what a profile's attributes do for a choice.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cmp
#| fig-cap: "Held-out IMV over a weighted coin: profile attributes in conjoint experiments, item difficulties in dichotomous IRW tables. One point per table; the diamond marks the median."

meds <- both |> group_by(family) |> summarise(m = median(imv))
p2 <- ggplot(both, aes(imv, family, text = paste0(table, "<br>IMV = ", round(imv, 3), "<br>", detail))) +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = family), height = 0.2, width = 0, alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = meds, aes(m, family), inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 23, size = 4,
             fill = "white", colour = "black", stroke = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = irw_grey) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(irw_red, irw_blue), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "IMV over a weighted coin", y = NULL)
ggplotly(p2, tooltip = "text")
```

Two things keep that gap from being a like-for-like contest between designs.
The first is the baseline. A forced choice between two randomly built profiles
is a coin flip by construction, so the baseline accuracy is almost exactly
`r round(100 * q1_wb)`%, and any predictive signal has room to show. Items are
not balanced that way: the median dichotomous table here is already right
`r round(100 * irt_wb)`% of the time by always guessing the more common
response, and relative gains over a baseline that good are necessarily smaller
(the item model reaches `r round(100 * irt_w)`%). The second is what the
features are. A conjoint's attributes are the whole stimulus, varied on purpose
across the range the designer chose; an item's difficulty is one number
summarising a question somebody wrote for other reasons. A conjoint is, in
effect, an experiment built to make the stimulus matter, and the comparison
shows how much that design choice buys.

### Which experiments are the attributes good for?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-object
#| echo: false

obj_lab <- c(person = "People", policy = "Policies", scenario = "Scenarios",
             product_service = "Products and services", place = "Places",
             organisation = "Organisations", message = "Messages")
by_obj <- q1 |>
  filter(choice_object %in% names(obj_lab)) |>
  group_by(choice_object) |>
  summarise(n = n(), med = median(imv_attr), w = median(w_attr), wb = median(w_base)) |>
  arrange(desc(med)) |>
  transmute(`What is being chosen` = unname(obj_lab[choice_object]), Experiments = n,
            `Median IMV` = round(med, 2),
            `Median held-out accuracy` = paste0(round(100 * w), "% (from ", round(100 * wb), "%)"))
knitr::kable(by_obj)
```

The conjoint literature is dominated by choices between people -- candidates,
immigrants, job applicants -- and between policies, but those are not where the
attributes do the most work. Choices between things, places to live and
products to buy, are the most predictable, and choices between policies and
between political messages the least. A plausible reading is that a profile's
attributes come closer to exhausting what there is to know about a product than
about a policy or a candidate, where what a respondent brings to the choice
matters more.

Even so, the differences between kinds of choice are small next to the
variation within them, and that is the more striking fact. At the top,
`r q1_hi$table` reaches an IMV of `r round(q1_hi$imv_attr, 2)`, predicting
held-out choices `r round(100 * q1_hi$w_attr)`% of the time from
`r q1_hi$n_attr` attributes; at the bottom, `r sum(q1$imv_attr <= 0)`
experiments with designs of much the same size do not beat a weighted coin at
all. What the attributes explain is a property of the particular experiment,
not of the method.

## Limitations

- **One model of the attributes.** The model is additive in the attribute
  dummies with a single ridge penalty, so interactions between attributes, and
  the restrictions some designs place on which combinations can appear, are
  only approximated. A model that used them would predict somewhat better, so
  these numbers are a floor on what the attributes can do.
- **Comparing two designs, not two estimates.** The conjoint and item-response
  numbers are the same calculation, but their baselines are not equally easy to
  beat (a forced choice starts at `r round(100 * q1_wb)`%, the median
  dichotomous item table at `r round(100 * irt_wb)`%), and item difficulty is a
  thinner description of an item than a profile's attributes are of a profile.
  Read the gap as a difference between kinds of design, not as a measurement of
  one quantity in two places.
- **A random, unmatched item sample.** The `r nrow(irt_df)` item-response
  tables are a random draw from dichotomous core tables, not matched to the
  conjoint experiments by sample, domain or length.
- **Forced choices only.** Ratings, opt-out tasks and designs with one or three
  profiles are left out, as are tables with fewer than 500 usable tasks. The
  screen keeps `r nrow(q1)` of the `r r_n_conj` conjoint tables in IRW.
- **Zero and negative values are kept.** `r sum(q1$imv_attr < 0)` conjoint
  tables come out slightly below zero, where the attribute model predicts
  held-out respondents worse than the training base rate does, and
  `r sum(abs(q1$imv_attr) < 1e-12)` come out at exactly zero, where neither
  model beats a fair coin and the IMV's accuracy scale floors both at 50%.
  They are left in, since dropping them would bias the median upward.
- **One version of the source.** Everything here is `irw_conjoint` v4.2 and
  `irw_conjoint_2` v1.4. Later versions will add experiments; rerunning means
  changing the version strings at the top of `conjoint_compute.R`.
- **One table left out.** `joo_2026_descriptive_rep` meets the criteria but is
  excluded: in its deposit every respondent's chosen candidate has the same
  position in all six tasks, so its outcomes do not line up with its profiles.
- **The widget.** Each experiment ships a random 250 of its tasks, and the
  estimator is a simple difference in choice rates rather than a model. Its
  reference points are the published AMCEs for the immigration experiment and
  the same simple difference over all respondents for the other three, whose
  standard errors, unlike the published ones, ignore the clustering of tasks
  within a respondent. The four experiments were chosen to be readable and to
  spread across the range of results, so they are not a random sample of IRW.
